title: Groin pain in a distance runner
objective: Recognize stress fractures as overload injuries, 0.7% to 20% of sports medicine clinic injuries; flag high-risk sites (femoral neck, anterior tibia, tarsal navicular, talus, sesamoids, 5th metatarsal)
secondaryObjectives: Explain the female athlete triad as low energy availability (intake that falls short of what training burns, with or without an eating disorder) combined with menstrual disorder and reduced bone mineral density

brief.situation: 14:00 in a university sports medicine clinic. You are the sports physical therapist. Sofia, 19, a cross-country runner, was referred by the team's athletic trainer for 'hip flexor strain, rehab please'. She has increased her mileage by half this season for the conference championship in 10 days.
handover: She has not had a period for five months and says she has 'cut back on carbs' to race lighter.
Clinic policy: a suspected high-risk stress fracture is made non-weight bearing and referred to the team physician for same-day imaging.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What does Sofia have, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Overload: a 50% mileage jump, night pain, end-range pain and a positive fulcrum test suggest a femoral neck stress fracture, a high-risk site; amenorrhea and restricted intake point to the female athlete triad and low bone density.
parts.modelAnswer: It's not a strain. A big mileage jump, night pain and a positive fulcrum test mean a femoral neck stress fracture, which is high-risk. The missed periods and dieting are the triad, which means weak bone.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Non-weight bearing on crutches, no hop or loading tests, same-day physician referral for MRI, and referral for nutrition and bone density.
parts.modelAnswer: Crutches, no weight, no hop test, call the team doc for a same-day MRI, and get her to the dietitian and bone density testing.

displaced.headline: Displaced femoral neck fracture
displaced.body: Groin pain with night ache, a training jump and amenorrhea in a runner is a femoral neck stress fracture until proven otherwise: non-weight bearing and same-day imaging; never hop-test it.

safe.headline: Protected and referred
safe.body: You took the triad history, examined gently, kept her off the leg, avoided loading tests and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Check whether she was loaded, whether the menstrual and diet history was taken, and how soon you called.

scoring.modelReasoning: Stress fractures are overload injuries; the femoral neck is a high-risk site because a fracture can complete and displace. Sofia's training jump, night pain, pain at end-range rotation and positive fulcrum test make it likely. Make her non-weight bearing, avoid hop and loading tests, and refer her for same-day imaging. Her amenorrhea and restricted intake are the female athlete triad (low energy availability, menstrual disorder, reduced bone density), which raises fracture risk and needs nutrition and bone health care.
